title: Common sunflower
wiki_lead:
The common sunflower (Helianthus annuus) is a large annual forb in the daisy family Asteraceae. The most common varieties have large yellow orange flowers heads, that are a tall stem. The flowers produce seeds in a floret, that follows the fibonacci sequence. The domesticated form of common sunflower is harvested for its edible seeds, which come in two types: oil and confectionery seeds. 
Oilseed sunflowers are widely grown globally and represent the fourth most used vegetable oil in the world. They also are used widely as bird food or as food for livestock.  In contrast, confectionery sunflower seeds are often eaten as a snack food or in baking. Though first domesticate in the Americas, production of sunflowers commercially is concentrated in Russia, Ukraine, and the European Union. 
There also are horticultural sunflower varieties that are used as plantings in domestic gardens for aesthetics. In some cultivation practices sunflowers are used for phytoremediation, removing chemicals from the soil, and as cover crop because root exudates help with suppression of certain kinds of weeds. Wild plants are known for their multiple flower heads, whereas the domestic sunflower often possesses a single large flower head atop an unbranched stem.

Wild plants are known for their multiple flower heads, whereas the domestic sunflower often possesses a single large flower head atop an unbranched stem.


Description
The plant has an erect rough-hairy stem, reaching typical heights of 3 metres (10 feet). The tallest sunflower on record achieved 10.9 m (35 ft 9 in). Sunflower leaves are broad, coarsely toothed, rough and mostly alternate; those near the bottom are largest and commonly heart-shaped.


Flower
The plant flowers in summer. What is often called the "flower" of the sunflower is actually a "flower head" (pseudanthium), 7.5–12.5 centimetres (3–5 in) wide, of numerous small individual five-petaled flowers ("florets"). The outer flowers, which resemble petals, are called ray flowers. Each "petal" consists of a ligule composed of fused petals of an asymmetrical ray flower. They are sexually sterile and may be yellow, red, orange, or other colors. The spirally arranged flowers in the center of the head are called disk flowers. These mature into fruit (sunflower "seeds").

The prairie sunflower (H. petiolaris) is similar in appearance to the wild common sunflower; the scales in its central disk are tipped by white hairs.


Heliotropism

A common misconception is that flowering sunflower heads track the Sun across the sky. Although immature flower buds exhibit this behaviour, the mature flowering heads point in a fixed (and typically easterly) direction throughout the day. This old misconception was disputed in 1597 by the English botanist John Gerard, who grew sunflowers in his famous herbal garden: "[some] have reported it to turn with the Sun, the which I could never observe, although I have endeavored to find out the truth of it." The uniform alignment of sunflower heads in a field might give some people the false impression that the flowers are tracking the Sun.

grok_lead: The common sunflower ( Helianthus annuus) is a large annual forb in the Asteraceae family, characterized by a coarse, hairy stem typically reaching 1 to 3 meters in height, broad cordate leaves with toothed margins arranged alternately or oppositely, and prominent inflorescences consisting of 20 to 30 bright yellow ray florets surrounding a dense central disk of brownish tubular florets that produce abundant seeds. Native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, and adjacent areas, it thrives in open, disturbed habitats such as prairies, roadsides, and fields, where it reproduces prolifically via wind-dispersed seeds and exhibits traits like drought tolerance and allelopathy that influence local ecosystems. Domesticated by indigenous peoples of North America for food and other uses long before European contact, the common sunflower has become a globally significant oilseed crop, with seeds yielding 40-50% oil content prized for its nutritional profile, stability, and versatility in cooking, margarine production, biodiesel, and animal feed. Major producers include Ukraine, Russia, Argentina, and the European Union, where it occupies millions of hectares annually and contributes substantially to vegetable oil supply, though yields are affected by factors such as disease susceptibility and weather variability. Ornamental cultivars vary widely in size, color, and form, enhancing its role in horticulture, while wild populations support biodiversity as a nectar source for pollinators and habitat for wildlife.
